questions.question: What is the CAP theorem and how does it affect real system design decisions?
questions.title: CAP Theorem: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance Trade-offs
questions.direct_answer: CAP says that during a **network partition**, a distributed system must choose between **consistency (C)** and **availability (A)** — it cannot have both. Partition tolerance (P) is non-negotiable in any real distributed system, so the practical choice every datastore makes is **CP** (refuse writes during partition to keep data consistent — e.g., HBase, Zookeeper, MongoDB with majority writes) or **AP** (keep accepting writes and reconcile later — e.g., Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak). PACELC extends this: even **without** a partition, you trade **latency (L)** for **consistency (C)**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of CAP as it actually applies (only during partition), the CP vs AP trade-off, and real datastore classification.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating CAP as 'pick 2 of 3' in normal operation, or claiming a system is 'CA' (impossible if it's distributed across the network).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss PACELC for the no-partition case, explain that consistency itself is a spectrum (linearizability → sequential → causal → eventual), and give concrete examples (DynamoDB tunable consistency, Cassandra QUORUM).

sections.title: What CAP Actually Says (and Doesn't)
sections.content:
Brewer's CAP theorem (2000, formally proven 2002) states: **a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance**. During a network partition, you must give up either consistency or availability.

**Critical clarifications:**

- The trade-off only kicks in **during a partition**. In normal operation, a system can be both consistent and available.
- **Partition tolerance is not optional** — in any real distributed system across a network, partitions will happen (network blips, packet loss, AZ failures). So the practical choice is **CP vs AP**.
- A 'CA system' would mean a single-machine database with no network involvement — not a distributed system at all.
- **Consistency in CAP is linearizability** — every read sees the most recent write. Weaker consistency models exist (eventual, causal, sequential) and offer different trade-offs.

sections.title: CP vs AP — The Real Choice
sections.content:
**CP (Consistent + Partition-tolerant):**
- During partition, the minority side **refuses writes** (or reads, or both) to avoid divergence.
- Examples: **Zookeeper, etcd, HBase, MongoDB with majority writes, Cloud Spanner, CockroachDB**.
- Use when: correctness > availability — financial ledgers, leader election, configuration store, distributed locks.

**AP (Available + Partition-tolerant):**
- During partition, **both sides keep accepting writes**; conflicts are reconciled later.
- Examples: **Cassandra, DynamoDB (default), Riak, CouchDB, S3 (most ops)**.
- Use when: availability > immediate consistency — shopping carts, social posts, view counters, sensor data.

**Mental model:** if losing a write or showing stale data is worse than refusing to serve a request, choose CP. If refusing to serve is worse than brief inconsistency, choose AP.

sections.title: PACELC — The Better Framework
sections.content:
CAP only describes behavior during partitions. **PACELC** (proposed by Daniel Abadi) extends it to normal operation:

> **If Partition (P)**, choose between Availability (A) and Consistency (C).
> **Else (E)**, choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C).

Even without partitions, a distributed system trades latency for consistency:
- Strong consistency requires coordination (quorum reads/writes, two-phase commit, Paxos/Raft) — adds round trips — adds latency.
- Eventual consistency means writes return immediately and reads can hit any replica — lower latency.

**PACELC classifications:**

| System | During partition | Normal operation |
|---|---|---|
| Cassandra (default) | AP | EL (low latency, eventual) |
| DynamoDB (eventual) | AP | EL |
| DynamoDB (strong) | CP | EC |
| MongoDB (majority writes) | CP | EC |
| Spanner | CP | EC (uses TrueTime for global consistency) |
| HBase | CP | EC |

**PACELC is more useful in practice** because most of the time your system isn't partitioned — you're choosing between latency and consistency every microsecond.

sections.title: Consistency Is a Spectrum
sections.content:
CAP's 'C' = linearizability (strongest). In practice, weaker models give meaningful guarantees at lower cost:

- **Linearizable / strong** — every read sees the most recent committed write, globally. Spanner, single-master MongoDB, Zookeeper.
- **Sequential** — all clients see operations in the same order, but not necessarily real-time order.
- **Causal** — if A causally happened before B, all clients see A before B; concurrent ops can interleave differently.
- **Read-your-writes** — a client always sees its own writes; other clients may lag.
- **Monotonic reads** — a client never sees the data move backward in time.
- **Eventual** — if writes stop, all replicas converge eventually.

**Tunable consistency:** Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB let you choose per-operation consistency:
- `R + W > N` (where R=read replicas, W=write replicas, N=total replicas) → strong consistency.
- `R = W = 1, N = 3` → eventual, low-latency.
- `R = W = N` → strong but high-latency.

sections.title: Real-World Examples by Use Case
sections.content:
**Financial ledger** (CP, EC):
- Spanner / CockroachDB. Refuses writes during partition; never lets two transactions believe both succeeded.

**Shopping cart** (AP, EL):
- DynamoDB / Cassandra. Cart writes always succeed; conflicting updates from two devices merge (union of items, possibly with quantity reconciliation).

**Service discovery** (CP, EC):
- etcd / Zookeeper / Consul. A stale service registration is worse than briefly unavailable registration.

**Social media feed** (AP, EL):
- Cassandra. Posts may take seconds to appear globally; brief staleness is acceptable.

**Distributed lock** (CP, EC):
- Zookeeper / etcd / Redis Redlock. Two holders of the same lock would be a correctness disaster.

**Analytics counters** (AP, EL):
- DynamoDB with eventual consistency, or Redis with periodic flush. Brief undercounting is acceptable; refusing increments is not.

**The pattern:** if double-spend or split-brain is catastrophic, go CP. If brief inconsistency is recoverable, go AP.

sections.title: How Datastores Implement Their Choice
sections.content:
**CP via consensus (Paxos/Raft):**
- Cluster elects a leader. All writes go through leader; replicated to followers via consensus.
- Quorum required for commits; minority partition can't form quorum, so it refuses writes.
- Examples: etcd, Zookeeper, CockroachDB.

**AP via replication + reconciliation:**
- Writes accepted at any node, async replicated.
- Conflicts resolved via:
  - **Last-write-wins (LWW)** — simplest; assumes synchronized clocks.
  - **Vector clocks** — track causality; surface conflicts to the application.
  - **CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types)** — mathematically guaranteed to converge (counters, sets, sequences).
- Examples: Cassandra, Riak, DynamoDB.

**Tunable in many systems:**
- DynamoDB: `ConsistentRead=true` for strong, default for eventual.
- Cassandra: `CL=ONE` (eventual), `CL=QUORUM` (strong if R+W>N).
- MongoDB: `writeConcern: 'majority'` for strong, `writeConcern: 1` for fast/eventual.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
sections.content:
- **'Pick 2 of 3' is misleading** — in normal operation you don't pick anything; you have C+A+P. The trade-off is only during partition.
- **'Consistent' doesn't mean ACID** — CAP's C is linearizability, ACID's C is database-constraint validity. Different concepts.
- **'NoSQL is AP, SQL is CP'** — false. Spanner is SQL+CP; DynamoDB can be CP (strong consistency mode); MongoDB can be either.
- **'Eventual consistency means never consistent'** — false; it means converges in absence of new writes.
- **'CAP is dead/over-simplified'** — partly true; PACELC and the consistency spectrum are richer frameworks. But CAP captures the essential trade-off well enough for high-level decisions.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CAP applies during network partition** — in normal operation, systems can be both consistent and available.
- **Partition tolerance is not optional** in distributed systems — the real choice is **CP vs AP**.
- **CP** = refuse writes during partition (Spanner, MongoDB majority, Zookeeper, HBase).
- **AP** = keep accepting writes, reconcile later (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak).
- **PACELC** extends CAP: even without partition, trade Latency for Consistency.
- **Consistency is a spectrum** — linearizable, sequential, causal, eventual; many systems offer tunable per-operation consistency.
- **Match the choice to the use case** — financial ledger CP, shopping cart AP, distributed lock CP, social feed AP.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**What CAP actually says**

During a network partition, a distributed datastore must choose between consistency and availability — you can't have both. Partition tolerance isn't optional in any real distributed system across a network, so the practical choice is CP vs AP.

**The most common mistake**

People say 'pick 2 of 3 in normal operation.' That's wrong. In normal operation a system can have all three. The trade-off only kicks in during a partition. And 'CA' isn't a real category for distributed systems — that would be a single-machine database with no network.

**CP vs AP — the real choice**

CP: during partition the minority side refuses writes to keep data consistent. Examples: Zookeeper, etcd, HBase, MongoDB with majority writes, Spanner. Use when correctness matters more than availability — financial ledgers, leader election, distributed locks.

AP: during partition both sides keep accepting writes; conflicts are reconciled when the partition heals. Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak. Use when availability matters more than immediate consistency — shopping carts, social posts, view counters.

Mental model: if losing a write or showing stale data is worse than refusing to serve a request, choose CP. If refusing to serve is worse than brief inconsistency, choose AP.

**PACELC — the better framework**

CAP only describes behavior during partition. PACELC says: if Partition, choose between Availability and Consistency; Else, choose between Latency and Consistency.

Even without partitions, strong consistency requires coordination — quorum reads, Paxos rounds, two-phase commit — which adds latency. Eventual consistency lets writes return immediately and reads hit any replica — lower latency.

Cassandra is AP-EL. DynamoDB default is AP-EL but can be CP-EC with strong reads. Spanner is CP-EC — uses TrueTime for global consistency at the cost of latency.

**Consistency is a spectrum**

CAP's C is linearizability — strongest. Below that: sequential, causal, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, eventual. Many systems offer tunable consistency per operation.

In Cassandra: `R + W > N` gives strong consistency. With N=3 replicas, R=W=2 means strong; R=W=1 means eventual but fast.

**Implementation**

CP via consensus (Paxos/Raft): leader election, quorum writes; minority partition can't form quorum so refuses.

AP via replication + conflict resolution: writes accepted at any node, async replicated. Conflicts resolved by last-write-wins (assumes synced clocks), vector clocks (track causality), or CRDTs (mathematically converge for counters/sets).

**Real-world matches**

- Financial ledger → Spanner / CockroachDB (CP, EC)
- Shopping cart → DynamoDB / Cassandra (AP, EL)
- Service discovery → etcd / Zookeeper / Consul (CP, EC)
- Social feed → Cassandra (AP, EL)
- Distributed lock → Zookeeper / etcd (CP, EC)
- Analytics counters → Redis or DynamoDB eventual (AP, EL)

If double-spend or split-brain is catastrophic, go CP. If brief inconsistency is recoverable, go AP.

**Recommendation**

**CAP captures the partition trade-off; PACELC extends it to normal-operation latency-vs-consistency. Real systems are CP (Spanner, Zookeeper, HBase) or AP (Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak); 'CA' isn't a real category for distributed systems. Pick CP when correctness is non-negotiable; pick AP when availability is non-negotiable. Many modern stores let you tune per-operation — so the architectural decision becomes which workloads need which knob.**
